title: Memorial Tower of Baengmagoji Battlefield in Cheorwon: A Beginner's Guide to Korea's 'White Horse Hill' War Site
html:
Most first-time visitors to Korea stick to Seoul and maybe a coastal day trip, so a stop like the Memorial Tower of Baengmagoji Battlefield is off almost everyone's radar. It's a Korean War memorial and small museum in Cheorwon County, a rural area in Gangwon-do near the DMZ (the buffer zone between North and South Korea). If you're interested in Korean history — or you're already heading to the Cheorwon border area for other DMZ sites — this is a quiet, moving place worth adding to your plan. Here's what happened here, what you'll see, and how to actually get there.

What Happened at Baengmagoji?

Photo: The Baengmagoji memorial grounds, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

"Baengmagoji" (백마고지) means "White Horse Hill." First, some quick background if you're new to this part of Korean history: the Korean War (1950–1953) was fought between North Korea (backed by China) and South Korea (backed by the United States and United Nations forces). It ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty, which is why North and South Korea are technically still divided today.

In October 1952, this hill became the site of one of the war's fiercest battles. Over about 10 days, control of the hill changed hands more than 20 times between South Korea's 9th Infantry Division and Chinese forces, with both sides repeatedly retaking it. South Korea held the hill by the end, and the division earned the nickname "White Horse Division" — the hill is said to have looked like a white horse lying down after the shelling stripped it of vegetation, which is also where the area's name comes from. It's remembered in Korea as one of the most intense battles of the entire war, and thousands of soldiers on both sides died here.

What You'll See at the Memorial

Photo: The memorial hall building, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

The site has two main parts: a tall memorial tower honoring the soldiers who died in the battle, and a memorial hall (small museum) with photos, maps, and items from the battle that explain what happened here in more detail, in a respectful, educational way rather than anything graphic. Most signage has English alongside Korean, since the site does get foreign visitors as part of DMZ-area tours.

Photo: The memorial grounds and monument, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

Outside, the grounds are quiet and well kept — a good spot to walk around slowly rather than rush through. If you continue a short drive past the memorial, you'll reach the Baengmagoji Observatory, a separate lookout point where you can see out toward the actual battlefield hill and the border area beyond it.

Good to Know Before You Go

Photo: The memorial's entrance area, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

Entry is free, and there's parking on site. Unlike the JSA (Panmunjeom) near Paju, which you can only visit through a specially authorized tour, this memorial is a normal public site — no passport check or advance booking needed to walk in. Opening hours and closed days vary a bit between sources (some say open daily, others mention closing on Tuesdays or public holidays), so it's worth calling ahead to confirm: +82-33-450-5559 (Cheorwon tourism info line, English available). Because this is a memorial for the dead, keep the mood respectful while you're there — it's not the place for loud group photos.

How to Get There From Seoul

Photo: The surrounding area near the memorial, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

Honest heads-up: this is not a quick trip. There's no subway or regular train service into this part of Cheorwon (the old "DMZ Peace Train" that used to run here stopped operating in late 2023), so your realistic options are:

  • Intercity bus + taxi: Take an intercity bus from Dong Seoul Bus Terminal (near Gangbyeon Station) to Cheorwon's Dongsong Bus Terminal, which takes roughly 2–3 hours. From there, it's a taxi ride out to the memorial, since local buses out this way run on a limited schedule.
  • Join a Cheorwon-area DMZ tour: Several operators run day tours from Seoul specifically to Cheorwon's border-area sites (as opposed to the more famous Imjingak/Panmunjeom tours near Paju, covered in our DMZ Tour Guide for First-Timers). These usually bundle Baengmagoji with other Cheorwon sights like the 2nd Tunnel or Peace Observatory, and are the easiest way to visit without a car.
  • By car: If you're road-tripping Gangwon-do, just set your navigation to "백마고지 위령비" or the English name — it's a short detour off the main road through Cheorwon.

Because this trip takes most of a day either way, it pairs best with other Cheorwon-area stops rather than standing alone — so if you're already planning a DMZ day from Seoul, ask your tour operator whether Baengmagoji can be added to the route.
